summary: This standards-track memo explains how TCP and UDP can use IPv6 jumbograms, packets larger than the usual 16-bit limit allows. It describes simple changes for UDP and for TCP's MSS option and Urgent field. It was replaced by RFC 2675.

plainLanguage.summary: A bigger moving truck needs the loading rules rewritten so the larger boxes fit.

subtitle: Adapting TCP and UDP to handle IPv6 jumbograms larger than 65535 bytes.

tldr.problem: IPv6 supports jumbograms (packets larger than 65535 bytes) through the Jumbo Payload option, but UDP has a 16-bit length field that limits it to 65535 bytes, and TCP's MSS and Urgent fields have the same constraint.
tldr.mechanism: For UDP, a length field of zero indicates the true length is in the IPv6 Jumbo Payload option instead. For TCP MSS, an MSS value of 65535 is treated as infinity (actual size determined by MTU discovery). For TCP Urgent Pointer, if the offset exceeds 65535, the packet is split into two pieces.
tldr.outcome: TCP and UDP can now transparently use jumbograms when IPv6 provides them, useful for high-speed networks and applications like video streaming or bulk data transfer. This was later superseded by RFC 2675.

today: RFC 2147 defined these extensions as a standards-track document. It was later updated and superseded by RFC 2675.

sections.title: IPv6 Jumbograms and Protocol Limits
sections.content:
IPv6 introduced the Jumbo Payload hop-by-hop option, which lets packets exceed the traditional 65535-byte limit. However, UDP and TCP were designed with 16-bit length and size fields that cap packets at 65535 bytes. UDP has an explicit 16-bit length field. TCP lacks a length field but uses a 16-bit Maximum Segment Size (MSS) option negotiated at connection start, and the Urgent Pointer field (16-bit offset) cannot reference data beyond byte 65535.

For high-performance networks and applications like video streaming or bulk transfer, this limits throughput. Simple changes allow both protocols to work with jumbograms while remaining backward-compatible.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv6 can carry huge packets, but UDP and TCP still think 65535 bytes is the limit. These are small changes to let them use bigger packets.

sections.title: UDP and TCP MSS Adaptations
sections.content:
For UDP, when sending a jumbogram (length exceeds 65535 bytes), the sender sets the UDP length field to zero. The receiver reads the true length from the IPv6 Jumbo Payload option instead. Checksum computation always uses the true length, never zero. This works because UDP's minimum valid length is 8 (the header itself).

For TCP, the MSS negotiation is simple: when the attached interface MTU exceeds 65535, set the MSS to 65535. If an MSS of 65535 is received, treat it as infinity and use MTU discovery to find the actual limit. The TCP window remains 16-bit, but the TCP Window Scale option (RFC 1323) can enlarge windows separately for high-speed links.
sections.plainLanguage: For UDP, a zero length field means "look in the jumbo option for the real size." For TCP, an MSS of 65535 means "as big as MTU discovery can handle."

sections.title: TCP Urgent Pointer Handling
sections.content:
The Urgent Pointer in TCP is a 16-bit offset that points to urgent data. If jumbogram data extends beyond byte 65535, the offset cannot fit. When the urgent-data offset exceeds 65535, the sender splits the packet into two pieces: the first contains data up to, but not including, the urgent data, with the Urgent field set to 65535 to signal that the pointer is beyond the packet. The second piece is then sent with the Urgent field set normally.

On the receiving side, when a TCP packet arrives with the URG bit set and Urgent field of 65535, the receiver treats the urgent offset as the length of the TCP data (byte 65535 + N in the next packet), not the value in the Urgent field.
sections.plainLanguage: If urgent data is further than 65535 bytes, TCP splits the packet in two: the first piece signals "urgent is further ahead," the second piece has the actual urgent data.
